problem: Learning-based mobile manipulation either restricts the action space, relies on demonstrations, or is task-specific, while MPC and planners are expensive and poor at reacting to dynamic or unknown environments. The prior LKF work also ignored obstacles and suffered configuration jumps.
motivation: Mobile manipulation needs joint base and arm motion, but defining whole-body motions is hard while end-effector motions in Cartesian space are easy to specify. Delegating base feasibility and collision avoidance to a learned reactive agent would let new tasks be defined without retraining.
key_idea: Decompose mobile manipulation into an arbitrary end-effector motion generator plus an RL agent that controls base velocity, torso lift and end-effector speed norm using a local occupancy map, with IK solving the remaining arm joints.
insight: The ablation on obstacle-free tasks shows each component adds success (PR2 avg 0.0 for LKF, 20.8 with BioIK/L2, 74.0 with learned torso, 81.6 with ee-velocity, 91.6 with collision/procedural training). Learning the torso removes most configuration jumps, and diverse procedurally generated training gives zero-shot generalization to unseen motions and dynamic obstacles. Pure end-to-end RL over the full joint space fails (0% on the 7-DoF robots), so the hybrid IK+RL split is what scales.
method: End-effector motion generator f_ee: any planner, imitation or spline system that outputs next EE velocities; it handles EE collisions only, not whole-body feasibility.

RL base agent (SAC): the observation is EE velocity, current and desired EE pose, goal, robot state, previous action and a two-resolution local binary occupancy map (0.1 m coarse, 0.025 m fine). Actions are base velocity, torso lift velocity and EE velocity norm.

IK with regularization: BioIK solves the remaining arm joints with a minimum-displacement regularizer, and the reward is a generalized kinematic-feasibility term (L2 position plus quaternion rotation distance).

Reward design: the overall reward is r = n_vel(λ_ik r_ik + r_coll) + λ_vel r_vel + λ_acc r_acc. It has a collision penalty of -10, a velocity-incentive term, acceleration regularization for smoothness, and penalties normalized per distance.

Procedural training environment: random rectangles and ellipses, random start and goal, with an A*-based obstacle-aware EE planner that keeps the EE near the base path. Training runs in a fast 'analytical' kinematic simulation without a physics simulator.
Robot-agnostic setup: one hyperparameter set is used for the PR2, HSR and TIAGo, and TIAGo training uses a base control frequency schedule; there is no HSR torso learning.

setting.backbone: SAC actor-critic with a small CNN map encoder plus MLP (~935k parameters, trained from scratch); IK via BioIK
setting.training_data: Procedurally generated random obstacle goal-reaching task in an analytical kinematic environment, 10^6 steps, 5 seeds; no demonstrations
setting.observation: Local 3 m binary occupancy map from LiDAR/range sensors plus proprioception and end-effector motion/goal
setting.action_space: Continuous base velocities (2 or 3 DoF), torso lift velocity and EE velocity norm; arm joints from IK
setting.privileged: EE planner has a ground-truth global map (except in dynamic tasks); MPC baseline gets a ground-truth SDF; the RL agent uses only local sensed maps (ground-truth in analytical env)

numbers.eval_set_note: 9 tasks, 50 episodes each, averaged over 5 seeds

numbers_note: No standard embodied-navigation benchmark; the results are on the paper's own mobile-manipulation task suite, reported as success rates (%). Per-task numbers are only partly listed here.
results: N2M2 reaches average success of 88.2/82.4/65.4% on PR2/HSR/TIAGo in the analytical environment, beating the MPC baseline (57.3/67.1/46.3) and E2E RL (0/28.1/0). Performance largely holds in Gazebo (79.2/82.7/62.8) and on real PR2/HSR (about 82.6%/78.6%). It also beats RRTConnect/Bi2RRT* on the PR2 and in the bookstore map (70% vs 22% or less).
limitations: No 3D or arm collision avoidance (only base collisions on a 2D map), causing failures at door frames and with head or arm self-collisions.
Relies on heuristic EE motions that can be overly restrictive, and independent low-level base/arm controllers limit precision; TIAGo (diff-drive) has much lower success from harder exploration.
Zero-shot sim-to-real without fine-tuning; centimeter-precision navigation remains hard.
builds_on: LKF (Learning Kinematic Feasibility, Honerkamp et al. 2021)
